categories.name: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities & CVEs
categories.summary: Multiple critical CVEs emerged today affecting AI development tools and infrastructure. AWS disclosed vulnerabilities in both Amazon Q Developer VS Code extension and Kiro GitLab tools, while a significant authorization bypass was found in NocoDB's MCP implementation. These vulnerabilities highlight the expanding attack surface of AI-assisted development environments.

key_items.title: Malicious Code in Amazon Q Developer VS Code Extension (CVE-2025-8217)
key_items.detail: AWS confirmed malicious code was distributed in v1.84.0, though a syntax error prevented execution and no customer environments were impacted.

key_items.title: Command Injection in Kiro GitLab Merge Request Helper (CVE-2026-0830)
key_items.detail: Maliciously crafted workspace folder names can trigger command injection; users must upgrade to Kiro 0.6.18 or later.

key_items.title: NocoDB MCP readAttachment Missing Ownership Check (CVE-2026-47388)
key_items.detail: Authorization flaw allows low-privilege MCP token holders to read attachments across bases and workspaces if they know the file path.

categories.name: AI Agent Security Research
categories.summary: Significant research dropped on AI agent security risks, with both academic and industry perspectives. A new paper details WebMCP tool surface poisoning attacks that can manipulate agent behavior at runtime, while CSA's assessment of 100 production agents reveals widespread security failures. The theme is clear: agent capabilities are outpacing their guardrails.

key_items.title: WebMCP Tool Surface Poisoning Attack Research
key_items.detail: Paper reveals how third-party scripts can inject or alter tools mid-session through registration races and metadata poisoning, fundamentally shifting trust boundaries from prompts to tool lifecycles.

key_items.title: CSA 'Lethal Trifecta' Agent Security Assessment
key_items.detail: Cloud Security Alliance found most of 100 evaluated production AI agents failed baseline security benchmarks, emphasizing need for end-to-end tool use and trust-boundary testing.

categories.name: Security Tools & Releases
categories.summary: Several security-focused repositories and tools were shared today, including Anthropic's reference harness for defending code and a new tool from TryNullSec. These releases reflect growing investment in practical AI security tooling.

key_items.title: Anthropic Defending Code Reference Harness
key_items.detail: Anthropic released a reference implementation for code defense mechanisms, providing a framework for security testing.

key_items.title: NullSec S1 Security Tool
key_items.detail: New security tool release from TryNullSec available on GitHub.

categories.name: Threat Intelligence
categories.summary: Open source malware tracking reports indicate the Miasma campaign has expanded to Azure infrastructure, representing a notable evolution in cloud-targeting threats.

key_items.title: Miasma Malware Campaign Reaches Azure
key_items.detail: The Miasma malware operation has expanded its targeting to include Microsoft Azure environments.

categories.name: Industry News & Resources
categories.summary: The monthly AI Security Newsletter for May 2026 was published and pinned, consolidating research, tools, events, and resources for the community.

key_items.title: AI Security Newsletter - May 2026
key_items.detail: Comprehensive monthly digest covering AI security research, insights, reports, upcoming events, tools, and learning resources.

top_insights: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is emerging as a critical attack surface, with both CVEs and academic research highlighting tool injection and authorization bypass risks in agent architectures.
AI development tooling (VS Code extensions, GitLab integrations) is becoming a supply chain attack vector, with multiple AWS-related CVEs disclosed in a single day.
Industry assessments confirm a capability-security gap: most production AI agents have real-world capabilities but lack proportionate security guardrails.
The trust model for AI agents is shifting from prompt-level security to tool lifecycle and metadata integrity—a fundamental architectural concern.
Cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure) remains a high-value target, with both AI tool vulnerabilities and traditional malware campaigns converging on these platforms.
